I think this is pretty easy to answer since there are so many civilizations out there. Things that appear in the vast majority of these civilizations are going to be linked to genetics in some way, things that vary radically or only appear in a small minority of the civilizations are probably social constructs. I also think it's important to compare cultures that have remained more independent from one another. European cultures, and consequently American, for instance have all built off one another very directly and in a [relatively] very short period of time, so even things that are social constructs might end up being shared between these cultures.

So for instance something that's not a social construct is religious belief. I think it's pretty easy to see why. People become self aware and one of the first questions they're going to wonder is how or where they came from. Lacking any sort of understanding of their world, let alone their universe, the answer is easy - magic. Why do things happen? Magic. Why happens when you die? Magic. Connect the magic and next thing you know people are engage in all sorts of strange rituals and flagellating themselves anytime something bad happens since clearly they've pissed off the magic. Of course on the other end religions themselves are obviously a social construct.

And on the other end something that is obviously a social construct would be pretty much anything related to sex. The standards here are so absurdly different from one culture to the next that it's fairly clear that everybody just builds up their own social constructs of normalcy. It's not so easy to come up with other examples that aren't completely self evident (style, government, social interaction, etc). At a time when it's said everything is a social construct, in reality I think very little really is.

Here's a curious one - technological drive.

Various cultures around the world have approached technology radically different. You have cultures around the world that technologically still live just a few steps away from monkeys. And that's at the same time that you have other cultures instantly communicating with each other around the world, running experiments on a space station that orbits the earth 15 times a day, and aiming to colonize other planets.

Our brains are fundamentally the same. The IQ of the 'less advanced' cultures tends to be lower, but the heritability of IQ is far less than the differences here so that's mostly going to be a red herring. In any case you don't need geniuses to start developing things like watermills or metallurgy. It's curious that it seems technological drive, something that seems to inherent and natural, might be to some degree a social construct.

Although maybe we can even see that in our own nation. Apollo 17 in 1972 was the last time the US put a man on the moon. But it's not only the last time we put a man on the moon but the last time we'd leave low earth orbit with a human up to present day 45 years later. It's entirely possible that if not for individuals like Elon Musk rekindling America (and the world's) space drive, we could have ended up going a century without leaving our planet's immediate orbit again. There have been of course many other technological developments made outside of space in the interim but I think that is clear evidence of a stall nonetheless that at least lends some credence to the idea that cultures' technological drive can and does wax and wane. In the opposite direction we went from the middle ages to the renaissance in a similarly brief period of time. Or similarly the Greeks had an very technologically and educationally developed civilization that was more or less lost for the better part of two thousand years.
